name: Taxila
info: Taxila is a city and World Heritage Site in the Rawalpindi District of Punjab, Pakistan, possibly founded around 1000 BCE as a capital of Gandhara and known in antiquity for its learning and its successive royal cities.

facts.founded: Possibly around 1000 BCE, when the first major settlement was established on the Hathial mound; the Ramayana says that Bharata, the brother of Rama, founded it and named it for his son Taksha.
facts.where: On the Pothohar Plateau of northern Punjab in Pakistan, on the eastern side of the Indus, about 25 kilometres north-west of the Islamabad–Rawalpindi area.
facts.known: A capital of Gandhara; surrender to Alexander in 326 BCE; the Mauryan governorship of Ashoka; the Indo-Greek, Indo-Parthian and Kushan cities of Sirkap and Sirsukh; a centre of learning with teachers and students such as Chanakya, Pāṇini and Charaka; Buddhist stupas and monasteries; devastation by the Huns
facts.today: Taxila is a city in Punjab, Pakistan, and its ancient sites have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1980.

t: Taxila grew from a settlement on the Hathial mound of about 1000 BCE into a capital of Gandhara, and it passed to the Achaemenids, Alexander in 326 BCE, the Mauryans, the Indo-Greeks, the Indo-Scythians, the Indo-Parthians and the Kushans.
It was a noted centre of learning for several centuries BCE, where each teacher ran his own school, and Chanakya, Pāṇini and the healer Charaka are among those linked with it.
The Huns devastated its Buddhist monasteries and stupas in the 5th century, and by the time Xuanzang visited in 630 the city was desolate and half ruined.
dyk: Its name was read by the Chinese pilgrim Faxian as "cut-off head", from a Jataka tale in which the Buddha, in a previous birth, gave his head to feed a hungry lion; a site called Sirkap still carries the same meaning.
ev: The first major settlement is established on the Hathial mound
Darius I campaigns in the region, and Taxila may by then have grown significantly
King Taxiles surrenders to Alexander the Great without a battle
The Indo-Greeks build a new capital, Sirkap, across the river
Inscriptions show Taxila under Kushan rule
The White Huns and Alchon Huns sweep over Gandhara and devastate the city's monasteries and stupas
Xuanzang finds Taxila desolate and half ruined

sections.origins:
Taxila lies on the Pothohar Plateau of northern Punjab, about 25 kilometres north-west of the Islamabad–Rawalpindi area. The region was settled by the Neolithic era. The earliest settled occupation in the Taxila Valley was found at Sarai Khola, where three radiocarbon dates suggest that the site was first occupied between the late 4th and early 3rd millennium BCE. Its deposits held polished stone celts, chert blades and burnished pottery. Kot Diji-style wares later appeared in greater numbers, and that phase dates from the mid-late 3rd to early 2nd millennium BCE. Ruins from the Early Harappan period around 1300 BCE have also been found, though the area was eventually abandoned after the collapse of the Indus Valley Civilisation.

The first major settlement at Taxila, on the Hathial mound, was established around 1000 BCE, and the city was possibly founded then. By 900 BCE it was involved in regional commerce, since pottery shards show trading ties with Puṣkalāvatī. Bhir Mound was inhabited around 800 to 525 BCE. According to the Ramayana, the city was founded by Bharata, the younger brother of Rama, and named in honour of his son Taksha. Its Sanskrit name, Takṣaśilā, translates as "City of Cut Stone" or "Rock of Taksha", and the modern name comes from the Greek rendering noted in Ptolemy's Geography.
sections.growth:
Gandhara was an ancient kingdom of north-western South Asia in the Iron Age, and Taxila was its capital. The Brahmanas, written between the 8th and 6th centuries BCE, preserve the name of king Nagnajit of Gandhara. Excavations show that the city may have grown significantly by the time of the Achaemenid invasion in the 6th century BCE. Greek historians who accompanied Alexander described it as wealthy, prosperous and well governed.

Under the Mauryans the city lay on the Grand Trunk Road, which joined the Mauryan capital at Pataliputra with Puruṣapura, Puṣkalāvatī and Central Asia beyond. In the reign of Ashoka it became a great seat of Buddhist learning, and one of his Aramaic inscriptions has been found there. After the Indo-Greeks founded Sirkap in the 2nd century BCE, local trade guilds controlled by the city minted most of its autonomous coinage during lulls in Greek rule.

Under the Kushans the city became well known for its trade links, which included silk, sandalwood, horses, cotton, silverware, pearls and spices. Kanishka founded Sirsukh, the latest of the ancient settlements at Taxila, and classical Sanskrit literature of the period shows it both as a centre of culture and as a militarised border city.
sections.rulers:
Taxila was sometimes ruled as part of the Gandhara kingdom, whose capital was Puṣkalāvatī, particularly after the Achaemenid period, and at other times formed its own independent district or city-state. It has been suggested that it was the capital of the Achaemenid province of Hinduš between about 500 and 330 BCE. In 326 BCE its king Taxiles, called Āmbhi, surrendered to Alexander the Great, who kept him in place as satrap. After Alexander's death in 323 BCE the partitions of Babylon and Triparadisus also recognised Taxiles as ruler of his realm, and the province is believed to have passed afterwards to Seleucus I Nicator.

Within a decade of Alexander's departure Chandragupta Maurya captured the provincial capital, and the Seleucid satrapies in South Asia were formally annexed to the Mauryan Empire after the Seleucid–Mauryan war. As told in Buddhist texts, Ashoka was governor at Taxila before he became king. In the 2nd century BCE the Greco-Bactrian kingdom annexed it, and several dynasties, among them one founded by Antialcidas, probably ruled from it. The Indo-Scythian chief Maues overthrew its last Greek king around 90 BCE.

Gondophares, founder of the Indo-Parthian Kingdom, conquered Taxila around 20 BCE and made it his capital. Inscriptions dating to 76 CE show that Kujula Kadphises, founder of the Kushan Empire, had captured it from the Parthians by then. In the mid-fourth century CE the Gupta Empire is believed to have had political influence there, and many Sasanian coins found at Taxila suggest some Sasanian control.
sections.life:
Taxila had a long reputation as a centre of learning, including the teachings of the Vedic religion and Buddhism. The Jatakas call it the capital of Gandhara and a great centre of learning with world-famous teachers, and show the importance of law, medicine and military science there. Students came from Kashi, Kosala and Magadha. A student usually entered at sixteen and studied the scriptures and the Eighteen Shilpas, which included archery, hunting and elephant lore. Sons of kings, nobles, merchants, tailors and fishermen are mentioned.

Some accounts treat Taxila as one of the earliest universities in the world, while others do not, since the teachers may not have had official membership of colleges and no purpose-built lecture halls or residential quarters seem to have existed, unlike later Nalanda. Each teacher formed his own institution, mostly in his own house, and no king or local leader controlled the teaching. Specialisation generally took about eight years. Fees were condemned, support came from society and wealthy merchants, poor students did household work in return for board and lodging, and gurudakshina at the end could be a turban, sandals or an umbrella.

Chanakya, the strategist who guided Chandragupta Maurya, is perhaps the best known name linked with the city, and the Ayurvedic healer Charaka studied and later taught there. Pāṇini, the grammarian, was part of its community, and Pali texts name Jīvaka, physician to Bimbisara, among its students. The Jaina tradition also holds that the Tirthankara Rishabhanatha gave Takshashila to his son Bahubali.
sections.crises:
The Kidarites, vassals of the Hephthalite Empire, invaded Taxila around 450 CE. The Gupta emperor Skandagupta repelled them, but the city did not recover, probably because of the strong Hunnic presence in the area, the breakdown of trade and the three-way war among Persia, the Kidarites and the Huns in western Gandhara.

Around 470 CE the White Huns and Alchon Huns swept over Gandhara and Punjab, causing widespread devastation and the destruction of Taxila's Buddhist monasteries and stupas, a blow from which the city never recovered. From about 500 to 540 CE it languished under the Huns ruled by Mihirakula, who presided over the destruction of Buddhist sites, monasteries and Hindu temples across the north-west of the subcontinent.

The Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang visited in 630 CE and found Taxila desolate and half ruined, with most of its sangharamas still in ruins and only a few monks remaining. He added that the kingdom had become a dependency of Kashmir, with local leaders fighting among themselves for power, and had earlier been subject to Kapisa. Later Islamic geographers such as al-Biruni named a region called Takeshar, identified with the general location of Taxila, which remained under the Odi Shahi dynasty until the Ghaznavids conquered it. According to the Jaina text Prabhavakacharita, the city also suffered a plague, followed by devastation by the Turks.
sections.legacy:
The site of Taxila was rediscovered in the mid-19th century. Pliny's distances had pointed to a place on the Haro river, but Alexander Cunningham noted that Chinese pilgrims, Xuanzang in particular, gave a journey of three days from the Indus, not two, and his explorations in 1863–64 at Shah-dheri convinced him that he had found it. Sir John Marshall excavated there over twenty years from 1913.

The ruins include four major cities of different periods, at three sites: Hathial and Bhir Mound, which date from the late 2nd millennium BCE to the 6th century BCE and from the 6th century BCE, Sirkap, built in the 2nd century BCE by the Greco-Bactrian kings, and Sirsukh, built by the Kushans. The area also holds Buddhist monuments, among them the Dharmarajika stupa, the Jaulian monastery and the Mohra Muradu monastery. UNESCO designated Taxila a World Heritage Site in 1980, citing the four settlements, which reveal the pattern of urban evolution on the Indian subcontinent over more than five centuries. The serial site has 18 components in all.

Taxila Museum holds one of the most significant collections of Buddhist stone sculpture in Gandharan art, from the first to the seventh centuries, much of it from Marshall's excavations. The modern city of Taxila, in the Rawalpindi District of Punjab, had a population of 136,900 in the 2023 census.

summary: Taxila, in the Rawalpindi District of Punjab, Pakistan, was possibly founded around 1000 BCE and became a capital of Gandhara. Alexander, the Mauryans, the Indo-Greeks and the Kushans held it, and it was known for its teachers. The Huns devastated it in the 5th century.
notes: START: the article says 'possibly founded around 1000 BCE' and the Hathial settlement c. 1000 BCE; it also dates Sarai Khola occupation to the late 4th/early 3rd millennium BCE, and neolithic remains to 3360 BCE. I used -1000 with circa true.
Only one article (taxila.txt) was available; no history article.

Dates of the Huns: the article gives Kidarites c. 450 CE, White/Alchon Huns c. 470 CE, Mihirakula 500-540 CE, and says Xuanzang visited in 630 CE (also 'between 629 and 645'). The intro puts Hunnic devastation in the 5th century.

Bhir Mound is dated '800-525 BCE' in History and '6th century BCE' in Archaeology; I used both loosely (800-525 BCE in origins; 6th century in legacy). Hathial is 'late 2nd millennium BCE to the 6th century BCE'.

No Mauryan key event: the article gives only 'within a decade' of Alexander's departure for Chandragupta's capture, no year; it is told in the rulers section. The Cunningham 'explorations in 1863–64' flag (1864) is the article's own range.
Article calls the Indo-Greeks' Sirkap 'opposite bank of the river from Taxila' (History) and 'built by Greco-Bactrian kings' (Archaeology); both given as in the article without reconciling.
Chanakya is said by the Buddhist texts to have hailed from Taxila; the education section links him with it. Charaka 'studied... and started teaching' stated as in the article.
Jain material (Prabhavakacharita plague and 'Turks' devastation') is attributed to that text; its date (2nd-3rd century CE) not stated in text of crises. 'Turks' as the article gives it.

dyk: Faxian's reading 'cut-off head' and Sirkap carrying the same meaning are stated in the article's Etymology.
The article says Sirsukh was built by Kushan rulers 'who ruled from nearby Purushapura' and elsewhere that Kanishka founded it; I used the latter.
